### Learning goals

#### This week

As mentioned in week 7, when you learned about shell scripts:

> The strategy you've learned so far, and that we will stick to,
> is writing scripts that run **a single program a single time**.
> We do this even though you commonly need to run a CLI tool many times,
> e.g. separately for each file or sample.
> That's because at OSC and other HPC systems,
> you can save a lot of time by submitting a **separate batch job**
> for each file or sample, since these jobs can all run simultaneously.

This week, we'll cover how you can submit your shell scripts as batch jobs.

#### This session

- Different ways to start "compute jobs":
  via OnDemand, with interactive jobs, and with Slurm batch jobs
- How to submit scripts as batch jobs with `sbatch`, and where their output goes
- How to specify `sbatch` options on the command line and inside scripts
- How to monitor and cancel batch jobs with `squeue` and `scancel`

## Compute jobs overview

Automated scheduling software allows hundreds of people with different
requirements to effectively and fairly access compute nodes at supercomputers.
OSC uses **Slurm** (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) for this.

As you've learned,
a reservation of resources on compute nodes is called a **compute job**.
Here are the main ways to start a compute job at OSC:

1. "**Interactive Apps**" ---
   Run programs with GUIs (e.g. VS Code or RStudio) in your browser through OnDemand.
2. **Interactive shell jobs** --- Start an interactive shell on a compute node.
3. **Batch (non-interactive) jobs** ---
   Run a script on a compute node "remotely": without going to that node yourself.

We've already worked a lot with the VS Code Interactive App,
and interactive shell jobs are covered in
[this week's optional self-study material](../bonus/slurm.qmd#interactive-shell-jobs)
(you should rarely need these).
What we'll focus on in this session are **batch jobs**.

## Basics of Slurm batch jobs

When you submit a batch job,
you ask the Slurm scheduler to run a script **"out of sight" on a compute node**.
While that script runs on a compute node,
you will stay in your current shell at your current node.
After you submit a batch job,
it will continue to run even if you log off from OSC and shut down your computer.

### The `sbatch` command

You can use Slurm's `sbatch` command to submit a batch job.
But first, let's recall how we've run shell scripts so far:

```bash
bash scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe
```
```{.bash-out}
First name: Jane, last name: Doe
```

The above command ran the script on whatever node you are on,
and printed output to the screen.
To instead submit the script to the Slurm queue,
start by simply **replacing `bash` with `sbatch`**:

```bash
sbatch scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe
```
``` {.bash-out}
sbatch: error: ERROR: Job invalid: Must specify account for job
sbatch: error: Batch job submission failed: Unspecified error
```

However, as the error message above ("_Must specify account for job_") informs us,
you need to indicate which OSC Project (or as Slurm puts it, "account")
you want to use for this compute job.
Use the `--account=` option to do this:

```bash
sbatch --account=PAS3493 scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe
```
```{.bash-out}
Submitted batch job 56603792
```

- This output line means your job was successfully submitted
  (no further job output will be printed to your screen).

- The number in this output is the **job ID**:
  a unique identifier among all compute jobs by all users at OSC,
  which you can use to monitor and manage the job.
  Each of us will therefore see a different job ID pop up.

- After submitting a batch job, you **immediately get your prompt back**.
  The job will run outside of your view,
  and you can continue doing other things in the shell while it does, or even log off.
  This behavior allows you to submit many jobs at the same time:
  you don't have to wait for other jobs to finish, or even to start!

#### `sbatch` options and script arguments

As was implicit in the command above,
we can use `sbatch` options _and_ script arguments in one command like so:

```{.bash .norun .syntax}
sbatch [sbatch-options] myscript.sh [script-arguments]
```

Depending on the details of the script itself,
any combination of `sbatch` options and script arguments is possible:

```{.bash .norun}
# No options/arguments for either:
sbatch scripts/printname.sh

# Script arguments but no sbatch option:
sbatch scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe

# sbatch option but no script arguments:
sbatch --account=PAS3493 scripts/printname.sh

# Both sbatch option and script arguments:
sbatch --account=PAS3493 scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

:::exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 1: Option order

What do you think would happen if you ran the following command?

```bash
sbatch scripts/printname.sh --account=PAS3493 Jane Doe
```

A.  The job is submitted and runs fine,
    just like when `--account` comes before the script name.
B.  `sbatch` fails with the "_Must specify account for job_" error.
C.  The job is submitted,
    but it prints "_First name: \-\-account=PAS3493, last name: Jane_".

Then, test your prediction by running the command.

<!----
<details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_</summary>

**B** is correct.
Everything after the script name is passed to the script as an argument:
so, `--account=PAS3493` becomes the script's `$1`,
and is not seen by `sbatch` at all.
Therefore, `sbatch` fails with the same error as above:

```bash-out
sbatch: error: ERROR: Job invalid: Must specify account for job
sbatch: error: Batch job submission failed: Unspecified error
```

If the account had been specified in some other way,
the job would have run and printed the output in option C.

</details>
---->

:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

### Where does the script's output go?

#### Slurm log files

Above, we saw that when you ran `printname.sh` "directly" with `bash`,
the script's output was printed to the screen,
whereas when you submitted it as a batch job,
only `Submitted batch job <job-id>` was printed to screen.
In the latter case, where did this output go?

It ended up in a file called `slurm-<job-id>.out` (e.g., `slurm-56603792.out`;
since each job ID is unique to a given job, each file has a different number).
We'll call this type of file a **Slurm log file**.

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>Getting this output in log files instead of printed to screen may seem inconvenient. Can you think of any reasons why we may not want batch job output printed to screen, even if it were possible?</summary>

_The answer will be added after class._

<!----
There are several reasons, such as:

- If you log off after submitting a batch job,
  any output printed to screen would be lost.
- The power of submitting batch jobs is that you can submit many at once ---
  e.g. one per sample, running the same script.
  If the output from all those scripts ends up on your screen,
  things become a big mess, and you have no lasting record of what happened.
---->

</details>

If you run `ls`, you should see a Slurm log file for the job you just submitted:

```bash
ls
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="ls-blue">scripts</span> slurm-56603792.out</code></pre>

Let's take a look at its contents:

```bash
# Auto-complete the file name with Tab: you'll have a different job ID!
cat slurm-56603792.out
```
``` {.bash-out}
First name: Jane, last name: Doe
```

This file contains the script's output that was printed to screen
when we ran it with `bash` --- nothing more or less.
That includes any error messages:
recall from week 4 that besides regular output ("_standard output_"),
commands can also print error messages ("_standard error_") to the screen.
In a batch job, both end up in the Slurm log file^[
Unless you explicitly instruct Slurm to print standard output and
standard error to separate files --- see
[this section on the optional self-study page](../bonus/slurm.qmd#separating-standard-output-and-standard-error)
for more.].

::: callout-tip
## The working directory stays the same
When the scripts in batch jobs are being run,
they start in the directory that they were submitted from:
that is, the working directory remains the same,
and you shouldn't have to make special adjustments to paths.
Additionally, as you've seen,
Slurm log files will (by default) be created in the dir you submitted the job from.
:::

#### Cleaning up the Slurm logs

When submitting batch jobs,
your working dir can easily become a confusing mess of anonymous-looking Slurm log files.
These two strategies help to prevent this:

- Changing the Slurm log file name to include a one- or two-word description
  of the job/script (next lecture).
- Cleaning up your Slurm log files, by:
  - Removing them when no longer needed --- as is e.g. appropriate for our current Slurm log file.
  - Moving them to the same location as other outputs by that script.
    This is often appropriate after you've run a bioinformatics tool,
    since the Slurm log file may contain some info you'd like to keep.
    (For example, you can move Slurm log files for jobs that ran FastQC,
    and produced outputs in `results/fastqc`, to a dir `results/fastqc/logs`.)

In this case, we'll simply remove the Slurm log file,
because it has no information that we need to keep:

```bash
# Again, auto-complete the file name to include the correct job ID
rm -v slurm-56603792.out
```
```bash-out
removed slurm-56603792.out
```

### Adding `sbatch` options in scripts

The `--account=` option is just one of many options you can use when submitting a
job, but is the only **required** one.
For all other options, defaults are set,
such as the amount of time (1 hour) and the number of cores (1 core).

Instead of adding these options after the `sbatch` command when submitting the
script, you can also add them **inside the script**.
This is a useful alternative because:

- You'll often want to specify several options,
  which could otherwise lead to very long `sbatch` commands.
- It allows you to store a script's typical Slurm options as part of the script,
  so you don't have to remember them.

These options are added in the script using another **type of special comment line**
(akin to the shebang `#!/bin/bash` line) that is marked by `#SBATCH`.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### Make sure the `#SBATCH` lines are at the top of the script _(Click to expand)_
Just like the shebang line,
`#SBATCH` lines **must** be located at the top of the script:
Slurm stops looking for them as soon as it reaches the first line with a command
(comment lines and blank lines before that are fine).
Any `#SBATCH` lines further down are silently ignored:
you won't get an error, but those options won't be applied either.

Another pitfall is a line that doesn't start with exactly `#SBATCH`,
like `# SBATCH` (with a space) or `#sbatch` ---
these will similarly be silently ignored.
:::

Let's add an `#SBATCH` line to the `printname.sh` script,
such that the first few lines read:

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/printname.sh (excerpt)" code-line-numbers="true"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=PAS3493
set -euo pipefail
```

So, the equivalent of adding `--account=PAS3493` after `sbatch` on the command line
is a line in your script that reads `#SBATCH --account=PAS3493`.
Now, you can run the `sbatch` command without options (which failed earlier):

```bash
sbatch scripts/printname.sh Jane Doe
```
```bash-out
Submitted batch job 56603905
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

:::{.callout-note}
#### `sbatch` option precedence!
If you specify the same `sbatch` option both on the command line and in the script,
the **command line option takes precedence**, so the one in the script is ignored.
This is sensible because it allows you to provide "defaults" inside the script,
and change one or more of those when needed "on the go" on the command line.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Running a script with `#SBATCH` lines in other contexts and on other computers _(Click to expand)_
Because `#SBATCH` lines are special comment lines,
they will simply be **ignored** (and not throw any errors) when you run a script with
them in other contexts.
For example, when you're running the script with `bash` instead of `sbatch` at OSC,
or when running it on a computer without Slurm installed.
This is convenient and means that these lines do not reduce the portability
of your scripts.
:::

## Monitoring batch jobs

Real batch jobs for your research projects may run for a while.
You may also be submitting many jobs at once.
Finally, longer-running jobs and those that ask for many cores sometimes
remain queued for a while before they start.
For these reasons, it's important to know how you can monitor your batch jobs.

### Checking a job's status

#### Batch job behavior

After you submit a job, it may initially be waiting to get resources allocated to it:
in other words, the job may be **pending**.
Eventually, and often very quickly, the job will start running.
You've seen this process with the VS Code Interactive App job as well.

Whereas Interactive App jobs will keep running until they've reached the end
of the allocated time^[Unless you actively "Delete" the job on the OnDemand website.],
**batch jobs will stop as soon as the script has finished**.
And if the script is still running when the job runs out of its allocated time,
it will be killed (stopped) right away.

#### The `squeue` command

You can check the status of your batch jobs using the below `squeue` Slurm command,
where:

- You specify your **username** with the **`-u`** option
  (without this, you'd see everyone's jobs!).
  In this example, I used the environment variable `$USER` to get your user name,
  but you can simply type your username if that's easier.
- The option **`-l`** (lowercase L, "long") will produce the more **verbose** output shown.
  Without it, the output will be a bit more cryptic, with abbreviations.

```bash
# Or: squeue -u jelmer -l
squeue -u $USER -l
```
```{.bash-out}
Mon Oct 26 14:21:34 2026
        JOBID PARTITION     NAME     USER    STATE       TIME TIME_LIMI  NODES NODELIST(REASON)
     56603512 condo-osu ondemand   jelmer  RUNNING      36:34   2:00:00      1 p0133
```

The output always starts with a line with the date & time and a header line with
all-caps column names.
Then, if there are any jobs in the queue, there will be one line per job.
In this case there is only one job in the queue, which is the **VS Code Interactive App job**.

Across the output columns, the following pieces of information about each job are listed:

| Column             | Explanation                                                                                          |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `JOBID`            | The job ID                                                                                           |
| `PARTITION`        | The type of queue (usually auto-assigned and not of interest)                                        |
| `NAME`             | The name of the job (by default the name of the script when submitting a script)                     |
| `USER`             | The username of the person who submitted the job                                                     |
| `STATE`            | The job's state, usually either `PENDING` or `RUNNING` (**_Finished jobs do not appear_**)            |
| `TIME`             | For how long the job has been running (here in "minutes:seconds" format)                             |
| `TIME_LIMIT`       | The amount of time you reserved for the job (here in "hours:minutes:seconds" format)                 |
| `NODES`            | The number of nodes reserved for the job                                                             |
| `NODELIST(REASON)` | -- When running: the ID of the node on which it is running.<br>-- When pending: why the job is pending |

: {.striped .hover}

### A sleepy script for practice

We'll use another short shell script to practice monitoring and managing batch jobs.
First create a new file:

```bash
touch scripts/sleep.sh
```

Open the file in the VS Code editor and paste the following into it:

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/sleep.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=PAS3493
set -euo pipefail

echo "I will sleep for 30 seconds" > sleep.txt

sleep 30s

echo "I'm awake! Successfully finished script sleep.sh"


```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Now, let's reason through a couple of variations on this, without actually
running them:

5. In terms of output files, what would be different if we instead ran the
   original script above using `bash scripts/sleep.sh`?

   a. Nothing: both `sleep.txt` and a Slurm log file would still be created.
   b. `sleep.txt` would still be created, but there would be no Slurm log file.
   c. No output files would be created at all.

   <!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_</summary>

   **(b)** If we had run the script directly with `bash`, `sleep.txt` would have also
   been created with the same content, but
   "_I'm awake! Successfully finished script sleep.sh_" would have been printed
   to screen instead of going into a Slurm log file.

   </details>
   ---->

6. Suppose you change the script's `echo` line to
   `echo "I will sleep for 30 seconds" > results/sleep.txt`,
   but the `results` dir doesn't exist yet.
   What would happen when you submit the script as a batch job?

   a. The job would succeed, because the `results` dir would be created automatically.
   b. The job would fail, and the error message would be printed to your screen.
   c. The job would fail, and the error message would be in the Slurm log file.
   d. The job would fail, but you'd only notice because `results/sleep.txt` is missing:
      the error message isn't saved anywhere.

   <!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_</summary>

   **(c)** The job will fail: `echo` can't redirect its output to a file inside a
   directory that doesn't exist, so this command will produce an error
   (something like _"No such file or directory"_), and because of our strict
   `set -euo pipefail` settings, the script will exit immediately at that point.
   You would find out about this in the Slurm log file `slurm-<job-id>.out`,
   which Slurm still creates by default in your submission dir --
   it will contain the error message.

   </details>
   ---->
:::

### Checking a job's output files

#### Two types of output

As you saw in Exercise 2, a batch job can produce output in two places.
These correspond to an important distinction between two general types of output
that scripts, commands, and programs can have:

1. Output that is **printed to screen**,
   both standard output and standard error.
   - Most shell commands, like `echo` in `sleep.sh`,
     by default print their output to the screen.
   - Other programs, like you've seen with FastQC, only print "logging"-type output
     (e.g. progress and error messages) to the screen^[
       But some programs will by default also print their main results to the screen.
       This can sometimes be changed with a program's options, and otherwise,
       you can always redirect (`>`) output to a file.].
2. Output that is **written to files**.
   - Programs like FastQC write their main results to files.
   - Shell commands write to files when you redirect their output,
     like the first `echo` command in `sleep.sh`.

Here is what happens to each of these when you submit a script as a batch job
instead of running it directly with `bash`:

| Type of output                    | Run with `bash`        | Submit with `sbatch`                |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Printed to screen (stdout/stderr) | Printed to the screen  | Written to the **Slurm log file**   |
| Written to files                  | Written to those files | Written to the **exact same files** |

: {.striped .hover}

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

In other words, submitting a script as a batch job only changes where
"screen output" goes, and not what happens to any output files.

Even if you've been monitoring a job with `squeue`,
you should always **check both types of output** to make sure it ran successfully:
the Slurm log file and any output files created by the script.

Let's keep things tidy and remove the script's outputs:

```bash
rm slurm* sleep.txt
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: callout-warning
### Be careful with deleting Slurm log files
If you delete a Slurm log file for a job that is still running,
the file will **not** be recreated when the job produces more logging output
later on.
That means that if you accidentally do this and the logging output is of key
importance to interpreting other outputs, or making sure it ran successfully,
you are better off canceling the job entirely and trying again.
[😕]{style="font-size: 1.2em;"}
:::

### Canceling jobs

Sometimes, you want to cancel one or more jobs.
For example, you may realize you made a mistake in the script
or used the wrong input files as arguments.
You can cancel jobs that are either pending or running using `scancel`:

```{.bash .norun}
# Cancel a specific job:
scancel 56604061

# Cancel all your running and queued jobs (careful with this!
# This also cancels your VS Code session, since that is a compute job too):
scancel -u $USER
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

:::exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 3: Cancel a job

Submit the `sleep.sh` script again,
check with `squeue` that it's running, and once it has been running for a few seconds,
cancel it with `scancel`.
Before checking anything, predict:

1. Will there be a Slurm log file, and if so, what will be in it?

   a. No: the job was canceled, so no Slurm log file will be created
   b. Yes, and it will contain the "_I'm awake!_" line
   c. Yes, and it will contain an error message from Slurm

   <!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_</summary>

   **(c)** There will be a Slurm log file, since the job had already started.
   It will contain an error message from Slurm like the one below,
   but not the "_I'm awake!_" line, because the job was killed during `sleep`:

   ```bash-out-solo
   slurmstepd: error: *** JOB 56604068 ON p0133 CANCELLED AT 2026-10-26T14:34:02 ***
   ```

   </details>
   ---->

2. Will `sleep.txt` be there?

   a. Yes
   b. No

   <!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_</summary>

   **(a)** Yes, because the `echo` line that creates it ran before the `sleep` command.
   (If you had canceled the job while it was still pending,
   neither file would have been created.)

   </details>
   ---->

Then, check your predictions,
and afterwards, remove the generated files.

<!----
<details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_</summary>

```bash
sbatch scripts/sleep.sh
```
```bash-out
Submitted batch job 56604068
```
```bash
scancel 56604068
```

Then, check for the output files and look at the Slurm log file.
Finally, clean up:

```bash
rm slurm* sleep.txt
```

</details>
---->
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Additional job management commands and options _(Click to expand)_

Here are some additional job management commands and options:

- Use `squeue`'s `-t` option to restrict the **type of jobs** you want to show.
  For example, to only show running jobs (and not pending jobs):

  ```bash
  squeue -u $USER -t RUNNING
  ```

- You can see more **details** about any running or recently finished job,
  including the amount of time it ran for:

  ```bash
  scontrol show job <job-id>
  ```
  ```bash-out
  UserId=jelmer(33227) GroupId=PAS0471(3773) MCS_label=N/A
  Priority=200005206 Nice=0 Account=PAS3493 QOS=pitzer-default
  JobState=RUNNING Reason=None Dependency=(null)
  Requeue=1 Restarts=0 BatchFlag=1 Reboot=0 ExitCode=0:0
  RunTime=00:02:00 TimeLimit=01:00:00 TimeMin=N/A
  SubmitTime=2026-10-26T14:38:44 EligibleTime=2026-10-26T14:38:44
  AccrueTime=2026-10-26T14:38:44
  StartTime=2026-10-26T14:38:47 EndTime=2026-10-26T15:38:47 Deadline=N/A
  SuspendTime=None SecsPreSuspend=0 LastSchedEval=2026-10-26T14:38:47
  Partition=serial-40core AllocNode:Sid=pitzer-login01:57954
  [...]
  ```

- **Hold and release** a pending (queued) job,
  which could e.g. be useful when you need to update an input file before the
  job starts running:

  ```bash
  scontrol hold <job-id>       # Job won't start running until released
  scontrol release <job-id>    # Job is free to start
  ```
:::

## Recap and what's next

In this lecture, you've learned the basics of submitting scripts as Slurm batch
jobs with the `sbatch` command:

- How to specify `sbatch` options on the command line or inside the script
- The basic behavior and outputs associated with batch jobs
- How to check the job queue, and monitor and cancel your jobs

In the next lecture, you will learn other commonly used `sbatch` options so
you can reserve more time, cores, etc. for your job.
You will also see some more practical examples of running batch jobs,
update your `CLAUDE.md` so Claude writes scripts for batch jobs,
and zoom out to look at whole workflows.
